units.outcome: Recommend an ethical response to a security conflict and explain the duty that governs it.
units.summary: Ethics gives a security professional a decision boundary when a request is legal-looking, urgent, or politically popular but would compromise people, evidence, or professional trust.
units.title: Professional ethics under security pressure

units.outcome: Classify a business consequence by its relevant security property and select a proportionate protection objective.
units.summary: Confidentiality, integrity, availability, authenticity, and nonrepudiation describe different protection outcomes. A sound decision identifies which outcome matters, to whom, and under what failure condition.
units.title: Frame security requirements with the five pillars

units.outcome: Explain who should decide, implement, oversee, and receive evidence for a security governance decision.
units.summary: Governance aligns security decisions with mission, strategy, risk appetite, legal duties, and accountable roles; management then implements and operates the chosen direction.
units.title: Govern security as a business accountability system

units.outcome: Identify the likely obligation category in a cross-border security issue and recommend a defensible next action.
units.summary: Legal, regulatory, contractual, and standards obligations create overlapping duties. A security leader identifies the applicable jurisdiction and obligation, obtains qualified interpretation, and turns it into owned, testable requirements.
units.title: Translate legal and compliance obligations into security action

units.outcome: Distinguish likely investigation types and identify the first evidence-handling and authority questions.
units.summary: Administrative, criminal, civil, regulatory, and standards investigations can examine similar events but have different authority, evidence, confidentiality, reporting, and escalation expectations.
units.title: Choose an investigation approach that preserves purpose and evidence

units.outcome: Select the correct policy-document type for a requirement and explain how it is owned, approved, communicated, and maintained.
units.summary: Policies set mandatory direction, standards make requirements consistent, procedures describe repeatable steps, and guidelines offer approved flexibility. Together they turn governance decisions into operational behavior.
units.title: Build an actionable policy framework

units.outcome: Use a business impact statement to prioritize a process and identify the continuity requirement and dependency evidence needed.
units.summary: Business continuity requirements protect prioritized business outcomes. A business impact analysis identifies consequences, recovery priorities, dependencies, owners, and acceptable disruption before teams select recovery solutions.
units.title: Set business continuity requirements from business impact

units.outcome: Recommend the lifecycle control that best addresses a personnel or contractor security gap.
units.summary: Personnel security applies proportionate controls from candidate screening through onboarding, role change, offboarding, and third-party engagement so that access, obligations, and accountability match a current business relationship.
units.title: Manage people-related security across the relationship lifecycle

units.outcome: Analyze a risk statement, distinguish treatment choices, and recommend the accountable next step with evidence.
units.summary: Risk management identifies and analyzes uncertainty affecting objectives, selects an authorized treatment, verifies controls, monitors change, reports residual risk, and improves the process over time.
units.title: Make risk treatment an accountable, continuous decision

units.outcome: Define a bounded threat-modeling exercise and prioritize a threat for treatment using system context rather than a generic threat list.
units.summary: Threat modeling systematically examines a system’s assets, actors, trust boundaries, data flows, threats, mitigations, and residual risks so design decisions are made early and revisited when the system changes.
units.title: Use threat modeling to improve a design before it fails

units.outcome: Recommend proportionate supplier or product assurance actions for a stated supply-chain risk.
units.summary: Supply chain risk management evaluates and treats risks introduced by suppliers, products, services, components, delivery paths, and dependencies before acquisition and throughout the relationship.
units.title: Manage supply chain risk throughout acquisition and operation

units.outcome: Design an awareness, education, or training intervention and identify evidence that it improved the intended behavior rather than only completion counts.
units.summary: A mature security learning program changes relevant behavior through role-appropriate awareness, education, and training, current content, realistic practice, reinforcement, and ethical measurement.
units.title: Operate a measurable awareness, education, and training program

units.outcome: Given a mixed set of information and technology, identify the owner and custodian, select a defensible classification, and explain what decision the label enables.
units.summary: Asset protection starts with a usable inventory and a decision about value, sensitivity, criticality, and ownership. Classification makes handling rules repeatable; it is not a label applied once and forgotten.
units.title: Inventory, own, and classify information assets

units.outcome: Design a proportionate handling rule for a classified asset and justify each control across its movement and use.
units.summary: Handling requirements translate an asset's classification and business context into actions for storage, processing, transmission, sharing, transport, access, and destruction.
units.title: Define information and asset handling rules

units.outcome: Specify a secure provisioning workflow that prevents unmanaged resources, excessive access, and configuration drift from entering service.
units.summary: Provisioning is the controlled introduction, configuration, authorization, and handoff of resources so that a new asset begins life with known ownership, secure defaults, and traceable approvals.
units.title: Provision resources securely

units.outcome: Trace a dataset through its lifecycle and assign ownership, controls, evidence, and transition criteria at each stage.
units.summary: Data changes state from creation and collection through use, sharing, storage, archival, and destruction. Each transition is an opportunity to preserve value and reduce exposure.
units.title: Manage the data lifecycle

units.outcome: Choose a retention decision and disposal method for an asset while accounting for legal holds, media, replicas, and evidence.
units.summary: Retention is a deliberate period and trigger based on business, legal, regulatory, contractual, and risk needs. Disposal ends authorized retention with a method appropriate to the medium and sensitivity.
units.title: Retain what is required and dispose of what is not

units.outcome: Translate a data classification and compliance context into layered administrative, technical, and physical controls with evidence and review criteria.
units.summary: Data controls should be selected from the asset's value, threats, lifecycle, and obligations. Compliance is a constraint and evidence requirement, not a guarantee that risk has disappeared.
units.title: Select data-security controls and compliance requirements

units.outcome: Recommend secure design principles for a stated architecture tradeoff and explain the failure they reduce.
units.summary: Secure design principles make security properties explicit before implementation: minimize privilege and complexity, separate conflicting duties, set safe defaults, layer controls, verify continuously, and account for shared responsibility.
units.title: Engineer security into design decisions

units.outcome: Select the model objective that best explains a proposed access or information-flow rule.
units.summary: Security models state a protection goal and formal rules for information flow or state change. They help an architect distinguish confidentiality, integrity, and conflict-of-interest objectives rather than treating models as interchangeable labels.
units.title: Use security models to reason about allowed information flow

units.outcome: Trace a security requirement to a proportionate control set, evidence, owner, and residual-risk decision.
units.summary: Control selection begins with business and security requirements, threat and failure analysis, constraints, and assurance evidence. A named product or framework is not a requirement.
units.title: Select controls from security requirements

units.outcome: Match a platform capability to a protection objective and identify the assumption that must also hold.
units.summary: Information-system capabilities such as isolation, memory protection, trusted execution roots, encryption, logging, and virtualization support security objectives only when their limits, configuration, and operational dependencies are understood.
units.title: Use platform security capabilities as architectural building blocks

units.outcome: Identify the dominant architectural trust boundary or failure path in a modern system and recommend a proportionate mitigation direction.
units.summary: Client, server, database, cloud, distributed, IoT, container, serverless, embedded, edge, and industrial systems expose different trust boundaries, management planes, update paths, and failure modes. Assess the architecture rather than applying one generic checklist.
units.title: Assess vulnerabilities across modern architecture families

units.outcome: Assess shared responsibility, orchestration, image, API, and serverless failure paths and recommend controls with accountable owners.
units.summary: Cloud service models, microservices, containers, and serverless functions change control ownership and multiply management, identity, image, interface, and event boundaries. Assess the specific provider-customer responsibility and the path from deployment authority to protected data.
units.title: Assess cloud, container, API, and serverless security paths

units.outcome: Assess IoT, embedded, edge, industrial, and high-performance constraints and recommend segmentation, identity, update, monitoring, and recovery controls appropriate to the consequence.
units.summary: Embedded, IoT, edge, high-performance, and industrial systems combine constrained update paths, long service lives, remote physical exposure, safety or availability consequences, and specialized interfaces. Security decisions must respect those constraints while reducing unauthorized command, data, and management paths.
units.title: Assess embedded, edge, IoT, HPC, and industrial-system constraints

units.outcome: Assess client, server, database, cryptographic, and distributed-platform boundaries and recommend mitigations tied to a stated failure path.
units.summary: Client, server, database, cryptographic, and distributed systems expose different administration paths, data flows, and failure domains. A defensible assessment names each boundary, the asset crossing it, the privileged control plane, and a mitigation with an owner.
units.title: Assess platform, data, and distributed-system trust boundaries

units.outcome: Plan justified cryptographic migration and evaluate quantum-related claims by inventorying dependencies, prioritizing exposure, and validating a controlled transition.
units.summary: Cryptographic agility is the governed ability to inventory, choose, replace, and verify cryptographic mechanisms as risks, standards, interoperability, and implementation conditions change. Quantum-related planning should distinguish current exposure, long-lived confidentiality, migration dependencies, and unproven or context-dependent claims.
units.title: Plan cryptographic agility and evaluate quantum claims

units.outcome: Select symmetric, asymmetric, hashing, and signature roles from protection requirements and identify a composition or implementation dependency.
units.summary: Cryptographic selection starts with the required property, data state, participants, trust model, performance, interoperability, and failure consequence. Symmetric, asymmetric, hashing, message-authentication, and signature mechanisms play different roles and must be composed into a managed protocol.
units.title: Select cryptographic primitives from protection requirements

units.outcome: Recommend a cryptographic solution direction for a protection requirement and identify the key-management or protocol dependency that could invalidate it.
units.summary: Cryptography supports confidentiality, integrity, authenticity, and nonrepudiation only when algorithm, protocol, key lifecycle, implementation, trust, performance, and operational recovery are selected as one system.
units.title: Select cryptographic solutions as complete systems

units.outcome: Design key and certificate lifecycle controls, trust validation, and recovery while identifying the authority and evidence for each critical transition.
units.summary: Keys and certificates create operational trust paths: generation, protection, access, issuance, binding, distribution, validation, rotation, revocation, recovery, archival, and destruction. An architecture is only as strong as the authorities and evidence governing those lifecycle transitions.
units.title: Design key management and PKI as trust operations

units.outcome: Distinguish brute-force, ciphertext-only, known-plaintext, frequency-analysis, and chosen-ciphertext assumptions and match each to a mitigation category.
units.summary: Cryptanalytic attack labels describe what an adversary can observe, obtain, choose, or compute. Brute-force, ciphertext-only, known-plaintext, frequency-analysis, and chosen-ciphertext reasoning helps an architect avoid claims that a mechanism is safe without considering keys, inputs, protocols, and implementation behavior.
units.title: Distinguish cryptanalytic attack models and assumptions

units.outcome: Classify a cryptographic attack path and recommend the mitigation category that addresses its decisive weakness.
units.summary: Attacks against cryptographic protection can target algorithm assumptions, protocol negotiation, key handling, implementation defects, side channels, authentication material, or availability. The correct mitigation depends on the actual attack path.
units.title: Reason about cryptanalytic and implementation attacks

units.outcome: Identify timing, side-channel, and fault-injection exposure and select mitigation categories based on the attacker’s observation and access path.
units.summary: A sound cryptographic primitive can fail when implementation behavior exposes time, power, electromagnetic, cache, error, or fault information. Implementation attack analysis locates the leakage source, attacker proximity, measurement capability, privilege boundary, and compensating design and operational controls.
units.title: Identify implementation, side-channel, timing, and fault-injection paths

units.outcome: Analyze intermediary, pass-the-hash, Kerberos, and ransomware paths as protocol, credential, endpoint, authorization, monitoring, or recovery problems.
units.summary: MITM, pass-the-hash, Kerberos exploitation, and ransomware combine protocol, credential, endpoint, authorization, monitoring, and recovery failures. Analyze the actual path and containment objective instead of misclassifying every problem as an encryption weakness.
units.title: Analyze intermediary, credential, protocol, and ransomware attack paths

units.outcome: Recommend facility design principles for a stated site risk while balancing safety, operations, and protection needs.
units.summary: Facility security begins with the business function, people, assets, threats, safety obligations, site constraints, and layers of deterrence, delay, detection, response, and recovery—not a list of physical devices.
units.title: Apply security principles to site and facility design

units.outcome: Select a coordinated control set for a facility asset and explain the response or recovery dependency that makes it effective.
units.summary: Facility controls protect wiring, servers, media, evidence, work areas, utilities, HVAC, power, fire, and environmental conditions through coordinated preventive, detective, response, and recovery mechanisms.
units.title: Design facility controls as coordinated layers

units.outcome: Identify the lifecycle activity that should produce or validate a needed security decision, control, or evidence artifact.
units.summary: Security is a lifecycle responsibility from stakeholder needs through requirements, design, implementation, integration, verification, deployment, operations, maintenance, and retirement. Decisions and evidence must survive transitions between teams.
units.title: Manage security through the information-system lifecycle

units.outcome: Given a network scenario, map the flow and architecture, choose proportionate segmentation and protocol protections, and identify the metrics and monitoring needed to validate the design.
units.summary: Secure network architecture makes flows, trust boundaries, protocol layers, planes, dependencies, and performance visible, then uses physical, logical, and micro-segmentation to constrain impact.
units.title: Design secure network architectures and segmentation

units.outcome: Select protocol, routing, plane, and performance designs that satisfy security and availability requirements while exposing meaningful operational evidence.
units.summary: Protocol and infrastructure choices determine reachability, protection, performance, and operational visibility across layered and converged networks.
units.title: Evaluate network protocols, routing, and infrastructure design

units.outcome: Design trust zones and segmentation controls for a network scenario, justify the boundary type, and identify bypass and failure evidence.
units.summary: Segmentation turns data flows, identities, and trust assumptions into enforceable boundaries that reduce blast radius while preserving required business paths.
units.title: Design network segmentation and trust zones

units.outcome: Assess a wireless, cloud, or remote connectivity design for trust boundaries, shared responsibility, resilience, and observable security controls.
units.summary: Wireless, cellular, satellite, CDN, VPC, SDN, and remote edges extend trust beyond the traditional perimeter and require explicit ownership, identity, path, and monitoring decisions.
units.title: Assess wireless, cloud, and remote network architecture

units.outcome: Evaluate a network component or endpoint and select controls for operation, media, access admission, maintenance, and failure conditions.
units.summary: Network security depends on the physical medium, infrastructure lifecycle, admission decisions, and host controls that implement the architecture.
units.title: Secure network components, media, and endpoints

units.outcome: Choose and operate a secure channel for voice/video, remote administration, data transport, or third-party connectivity while preserving identity, confidentiality, integrity, availability, and accountability.
units.summary: Secure channels align protocol protections, endpoint identity, remote-access design, collaboration use, data transport, and third-party obligations with the approved architecture.
units.title: Implement secure communication channels

units.outcome: Given an access scenario spanning a facility, device, application, and data set, identify the subject, object, action, control plane, owner, and evidence needed to permit or deny the request.
units.summary: Access control is the positive, reviewable control of subjects attempting to view, use, modify, move, or enter protected assets. A sound design coordinates administrative direction with physical and logical enforcement.
units.title: Control physical and logical access to assets

units.outcome: Given a human or service access need, choose an identity source, proofing and registration approach, authenticator factors, session controls, and accountability evidence that fit the risk.
units.summary: A trustworthy access decision begins with a stable identity, appropriate registration and proofing, and an authenticator whose assurance matches the consequences of compromise. Sessions, credentials, SSO, and nonhuman identities extend that strategy beyond the first login.
units.title: Design an identification and authentication strategy

units.outcome: Given an on-premises, cloud, or hybrid integration, identify the federation roles, trust artifacts, protocol purpose, assurance boundaries, and controls needed before accepting a third-party assertion.
units.summary: Federation lets separate security domains rely on agreed identity assertions or tokens, reducing duplicated accounts while introducing trust, availability, privacy, configuration, and vendor-governance responsibilities.
units.title: Use federated identity with a third-party service

units.outcome: Given a resource and access request, select or compare an access-control model, identify policy inputs, place the decision and enforcement points, and explain how the result is reviewed or revoked.
units.summary: Authorization translates policy into a permit, deny, or conditional decision for a subject attempting an action on an object. The model and enforcement architecture should express business authority, least privilege, context, and risk without relying on a successful login alone.
units.title: Implement and manage authorization mechanisms

units.outcome: Given a human or nonhuman identity change, specify the approvals, provisioning or deprovisioning actions, downstream revocations, elevated-access controls, and evidence needed to keep permissions accurate.
units.summary: Identity access must change with the relationship, role, task, and risk of a person, device, or service. Joiner, mover, and leaver controls, privilege governance, service-account ownership, and recurring review prevent orphaned access and privilege creep.
units.title: Manage the identity and access provisioning lifecycle

units.outcome: Given an enterprise authentication requirement, select an appropriate system pattern and explain how its directory, protocol, factor, session, accounting, failure, and revocation controls work together.
units.summary: Authentication systems operationalize identity and access decisions through directories, protocols, authenticators, sessions, and accounting. The design must fit the environment while protecting credentials, handling errors, and keeping authentication events attributable.
units.title: Implement authentication systems

units.outcome: Choose an assessment strategy for a stated control question and explain its scope, criteria, evidence, independence, and limitations.
units.summary: A sound strategy defines the decision, scope, criteria, independence, method, evidence, schedule, and limits before work begins.
units.title: Design and validate assessment, test, and audit strategies

units.outcome: Select and execute suitable control-test methods, preserve evidence, and interpret a result without confusing presence with effectiveness.
units.summary: Control testing selects procedures that reveal whether an administrative, technical, or physical control is designed, implemented, and operating as intended.
units.title: Conduct security control testing

units.outcome: Define useful security-process measures, collect reliable data, and distinguish a metric from a misleading activity count.
units.summary: Process data turns recurring control activity into measurable evidence about performance, exposure, compliance, and improvement.
units.title: Collect and interpret security process data

units.outcome: Turn test output into a defensible finding and report that states evidence, impact, likelihood, scope, limitations, and remediation ownership.
units.summary: Analysis converts observations into validated findings, risk context, priorities, and decisions; reporting makes limitations and actions clear to each audience.
units.title: Analyze output and generate useful reports

units.outcome: Plan or facilitate an audit with appropriate independence, evidence handling, interviews, sampling, findings, management response, and follow-up.
units.summary: Audits provide an independent, criteria-based examination of evidence and controls; their credibility depends on scope, competence, independence, and disciplined follow-through.
units.title: Conduct or facilitate security audits

units.outcome: Given a suspected security event, choose the lawful investigation posture, preserve volatile and physical evidence, document custody, and coordinate stakeholders without contaminating the inquiry.
units.summary: An investigation seeks defensible facts while protecting people, systems, evidence, and legal rights. The investigator must establish authority, preserve the scene and chain of custody, limit disclosure, and document actions so findings can withstand scrutiny.
units.title: Conduct investigations with legal and evidentiary discipline

units.outcome: Given a service and its risks, select event sources, fields, time controls, retention, integrity protections, and egress visibility that produce actionable evidence.
units.summary: Logging architecture makes security-relevant activity observable, attributable, time-ordered, protected, and usable without collecting everything indiscriminately.
units.title: Build logging architecture that preserves useful evidence

units.outcome: Given a service and threat scenario, select useful event fields and telemetry sources, protect and correlate the records, and define an alert or review path that supports response and investigation.
units.summary: Logging creates records of security-relevant events; monitoring interprets telemetry to detect deviations and guide action. Useful operations define what to collect, protect, correlate, retain, alert on, and review according to risk and purpose.
units.title: Design logging and monitoring activities

units.outcome: Given a detection signal, classify and prioritize it, select corroborating evidence, escalate or close it, and improve the use case without hiding meaningful risk.
units.summary: Monitoring turns telemetry, threat intelligence, and behavioral baselines into prioritized decisions while tuning controls to remain useful as systems and adversaries change.
units.title: Operate monitoring, detection, and alert triage

units.outcome: Given a system change or drift finding, identify the configuration item and baseline, assess impact, select an approved correction, and produce evidence that the resulting state is secure and reproducible.
units.summary: Configuration management keeps systems in a known, approved, and recoverable state. Inventory, baselines, controlled images, automation, versioning, documentation, and drift detection reduce the gap between intended and operational security.
units.title: Perform configuration management

units.outcome: Given an operational process, identify excessive authority, conflicting duties, missing service expectations, or unsafe staffing and propose controls that preserve accountability and continuity.
units.summary: Foundational operations make everyday security work reliable through need to know, least privilege, separation of duties, privileged-account governance, service expectations, and trained people who can escalate safely.
units.title: Apply foundational security operations concepts

units.outcome: Given a resource and lifecycle event, select protection, custody, handling, cloud-responsibility, and disposal controls that preserve confidentiality, integrity, availability, and recoverability.
units.summary: Operational resource protection covers media, equipment, cloud services, and supporting facilities throughout use, transport, storage, reuse, and disposal. Controls should follow classification, ownership, exposure, and recovery needs.
units.title: Apply resource protection in operations

units.outcome: Given an incident signal, prioritize safety and business impact, coordinate a defensible response, preserve evidence, choose containment and recovery actions, and capture lessons for control improvement.
units.summary: Incident management coordinates detection, analysis, containment, eradication, recovery, communication, and lessons learned so the organization limits harm while preserving evidence and restoring trustworthy service.
units.title: Conduct incident management

units.outcome: Given noisy or changing detection data, tune a control, measure false positives and false negatives, and automate only actions whose authority, safeguards, and rollback are explicit.
units.summary: Detection quality depends on coverage, control health, useful thresholds, analyst feedback, and automation boundaries that preserve evidence and prevent a defensive action from becoming a new outage.
units.title: Tune detections and constrain response automation

units.outcome: Given a threat and control objective, classify preventive, detective, corrective, and compensating measures, then define how they are operated, monitored, and tested.
units.summary: Preventive controls reduce the chance or impact of an unwanted action; detective controls reveal events or deviations so people or automation can respond. Operations must maintain, tune, test, and connect both types to a response path.
units.title: Operate detective and preventive measures

units.outcome: Given a threat and control boundary, select and operate an appropriate firewall, IDPS, allow or deny rule, service, sandbox, honeypot, or anti-malware measure with ownership and failure handling.
units.summary: Preventive and detective measures reduce exposure, identify suspicious behavior, and create response paths when designed for the boundary, asset, and failure mode they actually cover.
units.title: Operate preventive and detective control families

units.outcome: Given a vulnerability finding, prioritize remediation using asset criticality and threat context, choose a tested patch or compensating control, and verify closure without creating uncontrolled change.
units.summary: Vulnerability and patch management is a risk-prioritized operating cycle: discover assets and weaknesses, assess exploitability and impact, prioritize, test and deploy remediation, verify results, and handle exceptions transparently.
units.title: Manage vulnerabilities and patches

units.outcome: Given a proposed or emergency change, identify impact, approvals, testing, implementation, communication, rollback, monitoring, and closure evidence appropriate to the risk.
units.summary: Change management coordinates the business, security, technical, communication, rollback, and validation decisions that keep necessary changes from becoming unmanaged risk.
units.title: Participate in change management

units.outcome: Given a recovery capability, verify its copies and dependencies, operate failover or restoration safely, and collect evidence that resilience and recovery objectives remain credible.
units.summary: Recovery capability is an operating system of protected copies, replication, failover, resilience, capacity, and evidence that must remain usable as services and threats change.
units.title: Operate resilient recovery capabilities

units.outcome: Given a service disruption, choose a recovery strategy that matches business impact and recovery objectives, identify dependencies and alternate capabilities, and define how trust and service acceptance will be restored.
units.summary: Recovery strategies define how an organization maintains or restores critical services after disruption. They balance business priorities, dependencies, recovery objectives, resilience, alternate processing, backups, communications, people, and trustworthy return to operation.
units.title: Implement recovery strategies

units.outcome: Given a critical service and disruption profile, compare storage, site, and processing strategies against RTO, RPO, capacity, dependency, cost, and trust requirements.
units.summary: Recovery strategy selection converts business priorities and service dependencies into backup, alternate-site, and multiple-processing choices that can meet recovery objectives.
units.title: Select recovery site and processing strategies

units.outcome: Given a disaster scenario, sequence the disaster-recovery process, identify the people and dependencies involved, preserve decision evidence, and coordinate recovery without treating restoration as the whole plan.
units.summary: Disaster recovery processes turn an approved recovery strategy into coordinated preparation, emergency response, assessment, restoration, communications, and return-to-normal activities.
units.title: Implement disaster recovery processes

units.outcome: Given a disruptive event, coordinate declaration, response, personnel, communications, assessment, training, and lessons ownership without confusing technical recovery with business acceptance.
units.summary: Disaster recovery process governance gives people authority, sequence, communication, and evidence when an event requires coordinated restoration of prioritized services.
units.title: Govern disaster recovery activation and coordination

units.outcome: Given an activated DR event, sequence restoration, validate integrity and security, obtain service acceptance, and document residual risk and lessons.
units.summary: Disaster recovery restoration is a controlled sequence from assessment through rebuild, data and security validation, business acceptance, return to normal, and learning.
units.title: Restore and validate disaster-recovered services

units.outcome: Given a recovery plan and risk boundary, select an exercise form, define objectives and participants, and communicate test status without overstating what the exercise proves.
units.summary: A DR exercise tests a stated recovery assumption at a controlled level of disruption, with explicit objectives, scope, safety boundaries, stakeholders, communications, and evidence.
units.title: Design staged disaster recovery exercises

units.outcome: Given DR exercise evidence, classify findings, assign corrective action, communicate status, update the plan, and define a retest that demonstrates closure.
units.summary: An exercise creates value only when observations become accountable findings, corrective actions, maintained plans, and retests that improve recovery readiness.
units.title: Convert DR exercise evidence into maintained readiness

units.outcome: Given a recovery objective and test constraint, choose an appropriate exercise type, define success criteria and safety controls, capture results, and turn findings into verified improvements.
units.summary: DR testing provides evidence that people, procedures, dependencies, technology, communications, and recovery objectives work together. A test should reveal gaps safely, not merely confirm that a plan was read.
units.title: Test disaster recovery plans

units.outcome: Given a business disruption, identify critical functions and dependencies, select continuity workarounds or recovery priorities, exercise the plan, and capture improvements that protect the mission rather than only the technology.
units.summary: Business continuity keeps prioritized business functions operating through disruption by aligning people, processes, technology, facilities, suppliers, communications, and recovery priorities.
units.title: Participate in business continuity planning and exercises

units.outcome: Given a facility and threat scenario, select layered physical controls, define operational ownership and response, and verify that access, environmental, power, fire, and monitoring measures work together.
units.summary: Physical security protects people, facilities, equipment, media, and operations through layered deterrence, prevention, detection, response, and recovery controls that are maintained in their real environment.
units.title: Implement and manage physical security

units.outcome: Given a personnel or operational safety concern, choose a proportionate escalation, communication, protection, and continuity response that supports the person and the organization's duty of care.
units.summary: Personnel safety and security operations protect people from workplace violence, coercion, travel and duress risks, emergencies, and unsafe operational conditions while preserving dignity, privacy, and continuity of critical work.
units.title: Address personnel safety and security concerns

units.outcome: Select lifecycle gates and operational feedback appropriate to delivery speed, risk, and system change.
units.summary: Security continues through implementation, testing, deployment, operation, change, maintenance, and retirement; delivery method and maturity model shape evidence and feedback but do not remove accountability.
units.title: Integrate security into delivery and operations

units.outcome: Translate stakeholder risk into testable requirements and threat-informed design decisions.
units.summary: Security requirements and design decisions make risk, privacy, abuse cases, trust boundaries, and acceptance evidence explicit before implementation.
units.title: Turn risk into secure requirements and design

units.outcome: Place security activities and decision gates across an SDLC and explain how methodology affects timing, ownership, and evidence.
units.summary: Secure SDLC practices make security requirements, threat analysis, design review, testing, deployment, operations, and retirement explicit throughout development.
units.title: Integrate security into the SDLC

units.outcome: Design layered pipeline controls that produce trustworthy, traceable release artifacts.
units.summary: CI/CD, configuration management, repositories, artifacts, and application-security tests must preserve provenance and block unauthorized or untested promotion.
units.title: Secure build, test, and release supply chains

units.outcome: Apply access, isolation, inventory, and secret controls to the development environment.
units.summary: Developer workstations, IDEs, repositories, libraries, secrets, and collaboration services form a privileged ecosystem whose identities and boundaries must be protected.
units.title: Protect development environments and identities

units.outcome: Select layered controls for a development toolchain and explain how they prevent unauthorized change, leakage, and untrusted artifacts.
units.summary: Development ecosystems include people, repositories, build systems, dependencies, pipelines, environments, secrets, and deployment infrastructure; each can alter software trustworthiness.
units.title: Secure the software development ecosystem

units.outcome: Build an evidence plan that evaluates whether software controls reduce risk through development and operation.
units.summary: Software security is evidenced by requirements, design and code review, testing, runtime telemetry, vulnerability response, and outcomes over time.
units.title: Assess software-security effectiveness

units.outcome: Evaluate acquired software and services for trust, dependency, data, support, contract, and exit risks, then define controls and evidence.
units.summary: Commercial, open-source, managed, and third-party software introduce security, privacy, availability, licensing, support, and supply-chain decisions that must be assessed before and during use.
units.title: Assess the security impact of acquired software

units.outcome: Recognize high-impact coding and API weaknesses and select standards, design practices, and tests that prevent or detect them.
units.summary: Secure coding reduces common weaknesses by making input, output, memory, error, identity, API, dependency, and secret-handling decisions explicit and reviewable.
units.title: Apply secure coding guidelines and standards

units.outcome: Choose coding practices that prevent common source, API, authentication, authorization, and error-handling weaknesses.
units.summary: Secure coding prevents source-level weaknesses by validating inputs, encoding outputs, handling errors safely, enforcing authorization, protecting secrets, and using reviewable standards.
units.title: Apply language-neutral secure coding foundations

units.outcome: Identify implementation-specific failure modes and select prevention, detection, and containment practices.
units.summary: Secure coding also requires recognizing memory-safety, race, resource, dependency, and software-defined enforcement failures that vary by language and runtime.
units.title: Control memory, concurrency, dependency, and platform-specific failures
